item.title: The College Timeline
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

The College Timeline

Familiarize yourself with the core purpose of each year of college.

Posted August 25, 2026

There’s value in conceptualizing college not just as four years (or five!) all bundled together but as discrete blocks of time that each have their own purpose and characteristics. Each year marks a new transition and requires a different kind of courage and stamina. Try to begin each year with a few central, doable, and reachable goals, and review this each semester. As a professor for over 30 years and as someone who does speaking engagements on the college experience based on my book The Complete U: Over 100 Lessons for Success In and Out of the College Classroom, I try to describe to both students and parents how it's beneficial to think about the college timeline in this way.

Source: Deborah J. Cohan

Freshman Year: Arrange Your New Life and Make Yourself at Home

A beginner’s mind is often the best mindset. What is a beginner’s mind? It’s the ability to look with fresh eyes, to see what’s common and familiar in a whole new way. It requires openness and curiosity, two qualities that benefit all of us in higher education. Those who are beginners in anything bring with them more of a sense of a blank slate, a fresh canvas, and a way of seeing that is just insider and outsider enough simultaneously. Cultivating a beginner’s mind means letting the preconceived notions and judgments fall away, and it’s an openness to what is. Ripe with possibility, this mindset presents us with the opportunity to recreate ourselves every day.

  • Acclimate
  • Adjust
  • Reframe
  • Explore
  • Look into student organizations, clubs, and intramurals on campus, and explore activities in the surrounding community where you might meet new people and find meaningful activities.

Sophomore Year: Stretch and Socialize

Sophomore year offers a prime opportunity to enjoy present moment awareness. You’re not in as much of a rush as you might think. I learned this during my own sophomore year. You’re not that new, yet it’s still fresh. You’ve acclimated to some aspects and have so much more to discover and learn.

Half your friends aren’t scattered across the globe for study abroad, as they might be next year. And you’re not in the middle of graduate school applications or job interviews, and, best of all, no one yet is asking you nonstop questions about what you’re going to do when you graduate. Sophomore year is the time to solidify and deepen friendships that began freshman year and to let go of the ones that didn’t serve you as well, to move out beyond the ready-made social circle of roommates and dorm friends, and to chart your own course. The friends you make in college will likely carry you all your life.

Use this year to have conversations with professors, coaches, and others who might become potential lifelong mentors. They may help you connect with like-minded people on and off-campus. Students frequently share with me intimate details of their lives, and I’m constantly connecting them to other people who have been through something similar so they feel less alone and so they can benefit from peer mentoring as well. I’ve helped students who have lost parents or siblings, those struggling with various forms of self-injury, students who are faced with a new diagnosis of any kind, etc. When people are able to connect with a sense of mutual understanding and compassion about hard issues, that can be a beautiful thing.

article continues after advertisement

Hopefully, you’re more used to your surroundings, the college routine, and the rhythm of the academic year, and feel a bit more settled and grounded. That’s a great foundation from which to:

  • Stretch further and take risks.
  • Observe and deepen your passions.
  • Cultivate a strong social network of dear friends.
  • Connect with one or more mentors.

Junior Year: Focus and Fortify

Similar to junior year in high school, this is the time when things start to feel the most serious, but in fun ways. Things should gel more academically, as by this time you’ve likely completed general education requirements if those are necessary at your institution, and you’ve selected a major. During this time, the following will be front and center:

  • Focus your involvement.
  • Solidify your major if you haven’t yet done so.
  • Consider and seize potentially transformative experiences such as internships, volunteering, leadership opportunities, study abroad, or research with a professor.
  • Begin to think about all your options for work and future schooling, especially if you’re thinking you might want to start graduate work immediately after college.

Senior Year: Get Ready to Launch

You’ll be doing a new kind of individuating again, but this time hundreds or thousands of people will be doing it with you on campus as well as friends at other schools. Soon, everyone will scatter to different types of futures. Some may go after a job while others pursue graduate work, travel, or assume an internship, and to accomplish this, some may move back to their family’s home or venture somewhere entirely new. Whatever it is, it’s your launch!

Speaking of launching, I’m reminded of something. Years ago, when I was in graduate school, I discovered the figure skater Surya Bonaly. She’s known for launching herself into the air! Bonaly is famed for her back flip, in which she lands on one foot, an illegal move in the long program. Though I’ve never in my life attempted to even get on ice skates, Bonaly’s free-spirited ways resonate deeply with me. She marched to the beat of her own drummer, defied conventional guidelines, and risked the boldest, most daring jumps to be authentic. These qualities are important to witness when you think about composing your life.

article continues after advertisement
  • Cultivate your network.
  • Take full advantage of the community or city in which your school is situated, and tackle that bucket list before you graduate.
  • Keep all your options open before making decisions.
  • Connect with people in your chosen field for opportunities to gather more information, to shadow them, and gain experience.

Doesn’t this seem similar to the rhythm of a trip? The first few days are about getting adjusted; then it’s fun and relaxing, and you can just revel in being; then you realize all the things you still want to see, do, and accomplish before leaving; and then you have to plan your re-entry with your new lens on the world and a new sense of who you are because of the experiences you’ve had.

item.title: When the Immune System Walks Into the Therapy Room
item.description:
PANDAS

When the Immune System Walks Into the Therapy Room

New research on sudden behavior changes in children, and what this asks of adults.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Sometimes a child unravels in days, yet weeks earlier, there was a fever nobody noted.
  • Two studies published this year look at immune system activity behind a sudden change in a child's behavior.
  • Infections like strep can trigger brain inflammation without bacteria entering the brain itself.
Source: Mart Production/Pexels

There is a pattern I see so often now that I no longer treat it as unusual. A child who functioned normally begins to come apart. The change is fast, sometimes over just a few days. Food narrows, rituals appear, sleep breaks. A child who could read last month cannot sit at a desk. Somewhere in the weeks before, there was a virus, a sore throat, a fever nobody thought much about, or some sort of undetermined dramatic change.

The first place these families look is to a therapist, pediatrician, or psychiatrist, who, for the most part, would not consider neuroimmune root causes. Meanwhile, the inner storm continues to escalate, and no well-meaning intervention is likely to work. These clinicians would usually focus on social-emotional-behavioral root causes and miss what is right in front of them. This is not because they are not good practitioners, but because they are ill-informed.

How do I know this? I have been that parent. Even though I suspected neuroimmune root causes from day one, I was gaslit by clinicians who presumed to know what was going on with my kids, whom I knew best.

Why does it matter? Early intervention is critical, and in some cases these conditions can be reversed if treated soon enough. But if not, these conditions can become chronic, and it is my mission to help other families so they will not be impacted by this the way we were. Two recent papers are worth noting in this regard.

Neuroimmune Reactivity

I work within a framework I call neuroimmune reactive avoidance (NRA). NRA is a lens rather than a diagnosis. It asks us to read a child's symptoms, such as refusal, meltdown, or shutdown, as signals that the child's immune system is dysregulating threat signals. When the immune system is activated, when inflammation reaches the brain, when sleep is broken or sensory input is relentless, the body shifts into defensive overload. In that state, it is impossible for a child to engage with reason. An ordinary request, a transition, a shower, or a page of homework can push the system into fight, flight, or freeze-collapse.

NRA is not another name for PANS or PANDAS. Those sit inside the category. So do autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune conditions that involve the nervous system, dysautonomia, mast cell activation, and a much larger group of children whose OCD, restrictive eating, anxiety, or reactive behavior may have an immune contribution that nobody has looked for.

article continues after advertisement

The First Study, and Why Its Design Matters

A team led by Nishida et al. (2026) published a study in July comparing children with PANS (pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome) with those with other neurodevelopmental diagnoses.

Here is what makes this study useful. Every family filled in the same detailed questionnaire before anyone decided which group their child belonged to. Children with PANS and children with autism, ADHD, tics, or OCD were asked identically about history, family medical history, and what made symptoms worse. Only afterward were they sorted. What they found is more interesting than a list of PANS features.

Symptoms tended to appear early, around school age, and the flare looked different depending on the child's age. The youngest children lost speech, some going silent altogether. Older children became depressed. The same process showed up differently depending on where the brain was in its development.

The other important aspect in this study was that kids with PANS reacted more severely to ordinary triggers. This reflects a biologically vulnerable brain and immune system, rather than symptoms explained simply by stress.

Why this matters:

  1. In addition to medical treatment, intervention should focus on where the developing brain is/was when the onset took place and, as in trauma therapy, focus on methods that will help bridge the neurosequential gap created when the onset caused a developmental injury.
  2. Families should tailor an intervention plan that focuses on stress reduction and management until the child reaches baseline.
article continues after advertisement
How strep may affect the brain: The infection stays in the body. The immune signal is what travels.
Source: Based on Wayne et al., Nature Communications

The Second Study, and What It Shows Inside the Brain

The second paper explains how an infection outside the brain can change the brain itself. Dritan Agalliu's laboratory at Columbia published it in Nature Communications in August (Wayne et al., 2026).

Young mice were given repeated strep infections in the nose, week after week, roughly imitating the recurrent strep of childhood. The bacteria never entered the brain. Immune cells did.

Two things followed. The brain's blood vessels stopped maintaining their seal, so material from the bloodstream leaked into normally protected tissue. And microglia, the brain's own immune cells that usually maintain and prune connections, dropped that work and became inflammatory.

The team then measured immune signals in blood from children during an acute PANDAS or PANS episode. Several were the same as those produced by mouse brain cells. Why this matters is simple. It shows a physical route from a sore throat to a changed brain. Nobody has to argue that the child is imagining it, or that a firmer line would fix it.

The bottom line: This is mouse research with a small human comparison attached. It points to a mechanism and a possible target for future treatment, not to a treatment now, and whether inflammation causes PANDAS and PANS or occurs alongside them is still debated. It does, however, make the behavioral explanation much harder to hold.

Read together, the two papers meet in the middle. The first describes children whose symptoms swing with infection and stress. The second shows how that happens.

What This Changes in the Room

None of this makes a flare easier to sit through. A child in that state still cannot be reasoned with, because the part of the brain that handles reasoning has stepped back. Inflammation and fear reach the same destination by different roads, and the body's response is the same either way. The adult settles first. The child's body settles next. Talking comes last, once the thinking brain is fully engaged.

That is the work the NRA lens is doing. It diagnoses nothing. It reorders what we notice first so that a child's immune load is on the table before anyone suggests a behavior plan.

If you are living this now, I know what you are going through, because I have lived it too. Do not settle for an explanation that does not match what you are watching at home. Keep looking until you find a clinician who takes the immune picture as seriously as the emotional one. That kind of help exists, and with the right treatment, your child and all of you can truly heal.
